request: Tighten this explanation for a nontechnical teammate.
source: The reason the weekly total looks different from the sum of the daily numbers is that these two views are counting slightly different things, even though they both use the word visitors. In the daily view, a person is counted once on each day they visit. In the weekly view, that same person is counted only once across the entire week. So if someone visits on Monday and again on Tuesday, they add one visitor to each daily number, but only one visitor to the weekly number. This is expected behavior rather than a reporting error. We should update the labels to say daily unique visitors and weekly unique visitors to make the distinction clearer.
proposed_required_content: Daily visitors are deduplicated within each day while weekly visitors are deduplicated across the week
A person visiting Monday and Tuesday counts in both daily totals but once in the weekly total
The difference is expected rather than a reporting error
Recommend labels daily unique visitors and weekly unique visitors
draft:
Daily visitors counts each person once per day; weekly visitors counts each person once across the week. Someone who visits Monday and Tuesday adds one to each day’s count but only one to the weekly count.

That’s why adding the daily numbers can give a higher total than the weekly view. This is expected behavior. We should label the views “daily unique visitors” and “weekly unique visitors” to make the distinction clearer.

request: Teach a beginner what a database index does in 100–150 words. Use a familiar analogy, explain the read/write tradeoff, and include one practical example.
source: An index is an auxiliary data structure that can help a database locate matching rows without scanning the entire table. It consumes storage and must be maintained when relevant data is inserted, updated, or deleted. Not every query benefits from an index.
proposed_required_content: Explain locating rows without scanning the full table in beginner language
Include a familiar analogy
Explain that storage and maintenance make writes more costly
Give a practical example of a query benefiting from an index
Do not imply every query benefits
draft:
A database index works like the index at the back of a cookbook. To find recipes with potatoes, you can look up “potatoes” and jump to the listed pages instead of reading every recipe. Similarly, a database index helps locate matching rows without scanning the entire table.

For example, an index on a customer table's email column can help the database quickly find the customer with a particular email address.

That convenience has a cost. The index takes up storage, and the database must maintain it when relevant data is added, changed, or deleted. This adds work to writes, even as it can speed up reads. Not every query benefits, so indexes should support the searches you actually need.

A database index works like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up in the index and go straight to the relevant pages. A database can similarly use an index to find matching rows without checking the whole table.

request: Teach a beginner what a database index does in 100–150 words. Use a familiar analogy, explain the read/write tradeoff, and include one practical example.
source: An index is an auxiliary data structure that can help a database locate matching rows without scanning the entire table. It consumes storage and must be maintained when relevant data is inserted, updated, or deleted. Not every query benefits from an index.
proposed_required_content: Explain locating rows without scanning the full table in beginner language
Include a familiar analogy
Explain that storage and maintenance make writes more costly
Give a practical example of a query benefiting from an index
Do not imply every query benefits
draft:
A database index works like the index at the back of a cookbook. To find recipes with potatoes, you can look up “potatoes” and jump to the listed pages instead of reading every recipe. A database index similarly helps the database find matching rows without checking the whole table.

For example, an index on a customer table’s email column can speed up finding a customer by email address.

The tradeoff is extra storage and maintenance. When relevant data is inserted, updated, or deleted, the database must update the index too, which adds work and can slow writes. An index also won’t help every query: an email index may do little for a search by city. Choose indexes based on the searches your application needs.

request: Teach a beginner what a database index does in 100–150 words. Use a familiar analogy, explain the read/write tradeoff, and include one practical example.
source: An index is an auxiliary data structure that can help a database locate matching rows without scanning the entire table. It consumes storage and must be maintained when relevant data is inserted, updated, or deleted. Not every query benefits from an index.

Include a familiar analogy

Give a practical example of a query benefiting from an index
Do not imply every query benefits
draft:
A database index works like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up and go straight to the relevant pages. Similarly, a database can use an index to locate matching rows without checking every row in a table.

For example, if an app often searches for a customer by email address, an index on the email column can make those searches faster.

The tradeoff is storage and extra work when data changes. When you insert, update, or delete relevant data, the database must also maintain the index, which can slow writes. Not every query benefits from an index, so choose indexes based on the searches your app actually performs.
